title: Practical engineering advantage narrative
content:
TL;DR
Redwood wins when engineering teams need inference that behaves like a first-class, predictable service — not a research experiment. This brief frames a compact, engineer-focused positioning: mission, thesis, three messaging pillars, quick competitive map, and tactical headline options for developer-facing copy and sales outreach.

Mission (single line)
Make inference behave like core infrastructure: predictable, observable, and economical for product teams.

Thesis (why this matters)
- The competitive margin for AI shifts from model access to serving: shipping LLM features is now about consistent latency, controllable cost, and safe rollouts.
- Engineering teams adopt technology that reduces cognitive load: fewer surprise regressions, deterministic operational knobs, and transparent unit economics.
- Redwood is built for that reality: a runtime + orchestration stack that treats inference as infrastructure, with guardrails for reliability, cost, and experimentation.

Positioning pillars (copy-ready)
1) Predictable performance, not guesswork
   - Message: Ship features with latency SLOs you can commit to. Redwood gives latency percentiles, routing policies, and fallback paths so your product doesn’t fail when traffic or sequence length changes.
   - Evidence: per-route p95/p99 dashboards, SLA playbooks, automatic fallback to quantized variants.

2) Unit-economics control for builders
   - Message: Optimization is a product-first problem. We give devs deterministic levers (batching/caching profiles, quantization recommendations, model variants) so you can meet margins without sacrificing UX.
   - Evidence: case study bullets (e.g., 40% token cost reduction using auto-batching for a search reranker), Optimize suggestions engine.

3) Unified runtime across deployment modes
   - Message: Same API, same rollout primitives across hosted, dedicated, and private. Teams move from POC -> production without operational rewrite.
   - Evidence: migration playbook, Private control plane screenshots, compatibility matrix.

Buyer-facing narrative (two-sentence elevator)
Engineers: stop juggling model forks and incident runbooks. Redwood gives you a single inference runtime that guarantees predictable latency and transparent cost controls across hosted, reserved, and private deployments — so product teams can ship features reliably and measure unit economics precisely.

Competitor shorthand (working matrix / notes)
- Public cloud managed endpoints (largest clouds): strong infra scale, weak inference-first optimizations. Typical tradeoffs: high variability at token-level cost, limited runtime-level caching, vendor lock at API semantics.
- LLM API-only vendors: fastest onboarding but opaque unit economics and hard to meet enterprise SLOs when traffic spikes.
- Self-hosted inference stacks: ultimate control but large engineering tax (maintenance, kernel tuning, rollout guardrails).
- Redwood (position): middle ground — runtime tuned for inference, built-in operational guardrails, and migration paths to private deployments with lower engineering cost than DIY.

Key proof-points to surface (short bullets for one-pager)
- End-to-end p95 latency guarantees across supported workloads (demo data + slides).
- Customer example: mid-market SaaS reduced inference cost per session by 32% after adopting batching + cache policies. (internal case study id)
- Rollout primitives: canary + automatic rollback + A/B routing — used in production by two customers in compliance environments.
- Quantization profiles and kernel selection reduced GPU hours for long-sequence workloads by 25%.

Website and SDR headline options (iterative, pick 1–2)
- "Inference that behaves like infrastructure"
- "Predictable latency. Measurable cost. One runtime for every environment."
- "Ship LLM features with SLOs you can promise to customers."

Developer console copy snippets (short)
- "Per-route latency SLOs"
- "Auto-suggested batching & cache settings"
- "Pin model versions and run safe rollouts"

Open questions / debate points (please add)
- Do we want to foreground "cost" or "reliability" on the homepage hero? My take: reliability first for enterprise trust, cost as primary conversion for PLG flow.
- How granular should the public performance claims be? We can publish p95 numbers by workload class but not per-model microbenchmarks right now.
- Should we include a short DIY comparison (engineering hours saved) with a simple calculator on the site? Good for platform teams.

Tactical asks / next steps
- Product: compile three representative workload profiles (chat short, long-form generation, embeddings search) and generate p95/p99 reports. Target week: 2 weeks.
- Research: quantify CPU/GPU hours saved for two customers after Optimize recommendations. Add to case study. Target: 3 weeks.
- GTM: draft hero copy variations for A/B test on homepage and sign-up flow. Owner: Evan. Target: next week.
- Content: write a 1-pager for platform teams titled "How to make inference predictable" that includes migration checklist and ROI calc. Owner: Priya.

Notes to self / rough fragments
- Include calls to action for both "Try API" and "Talk to Sales" — we need conversion paths for PLG and enterprise.
- Link to RFC about routing policies (github PR above) — this is our engineering differentiation.
- Slack threads: #gtn-inference-lp, #benchmarks — watch for competing benchmark drafts (Diego).

Draft messaging variants for email outreach (for SDRs)
- Variant A (platform): "We help platform teams standardize inference across 3 environments and reclaim weeks of engineering work. Quick 15-min sync?"
- Variant B (product): "Ship the next LLM feature without unexpected latency spikes or token-cost surprises. See a short demo?"

Appendix: quick competitive detail (notes)
- Cloud endpoints: pros = scale, cons = poor token-level cost visibility, limited caching.
- API vendors: pros = simple, cons = vendor opaqueness + limited rollout controls.
- DIY inference: pros = control, cons = ops overhead, kernel-level expertise needed.
- Redwood: rails for ops + developer ergonomics.

Unresolved: add quantified claims only after product & research reviews. Keep this doc as working copy for messaging alignment.

-- Samira
